preview: Sahil Dhillon shares his successful interview experience for the 2024 summer internship (Global Markets) at Bank of America, detailing the resume screening, HireVue assessment, group discussion, technical interview, and HR round.
content:
Sahil Dhillon
TY IT
Interview experience for 2024 summer internship 
(Global Markets)

1. Resume shortlisting
This was the first time that this division of BofA had come to our campus. It 
started off with a resume screening round, after which about 70 students were 
shortlisted and invited for the HireVue interview.
Resume guide:
1. Be sure to add only relevant things in your resume and follow the latex 
overleaf template provided by TPO, which parses well with the ATS. You 
never know whether it’s being read by a person or AI. Avoid using fancy 
templates.
2. Don’t try to force too many cookie-cutter projects in the resume. If you 
really need to, then it’s fine, but try to make it such that each project is very 
dense, covers a lot of functionality, and shows that you’ve put in a lot of 
effort and learned many new things while making it. 
For example, you may have built a text summarizer and tag extractor 
using NLP and a separate e-commerce application. You can merge these 
projects together! Show a combined summary of every review provided 
by users using your text summariser. Amazon recently added this feature:
This would show that you have the ability to mix technologies of 
various domains together and can actually apply your knowledge to 
provide a meaningful solution.
3. Do NOT lie on your resume. If it was a team project, mention the parts you 
worked on. The interviewers can very easily determine whether a project 
was made by you or not and call your bluff. It’s simply not worth it. Add all 
your work sincerely and be ready to explain the implementation details in 
depth. If you have added extracurricular activities, be sure to prepare 
common questions for those as well (Eg. why did you join this committee, 
what conflicts did you face, what did you learn).
The STAR method is a structured approach commonly used to answer 
behavioral interview questions, and it can also be applied to explain 
projects or experiences in a clear and organized manner. 
I also used to watch resume review videos to gain more clarity, like this one.
2. HireVue
I had previously given one for JPMC, but could not clear it because I took it lightly 
and fumbled. I was determined to ace it this time.
You have to record video responses to some questions. Make sure you are 
dressed well, are sitting in proper lighting, and speak loudly and clearly. I watched 
a lot of videos like this to prepare well. Last time, I forgot a lot in between 
because I didn’t properly practice speaking without looking. So record yourself 
speaking these answers fully as if you are sitting in the actual interview.
We had a total of 5 questions. The first two questions were behavioral:
1. Introduce yourself and why did you apply for this role/ Bank of America. 
A pretty common question that gets asked everywhere. I had read the 
role requirements and mentioned, while referring to experiences, why I 
would do well in this role and some facts and products about BofA which 
I thought were very impressive, so I would love to be a part of this 
organization. Research about the company, the services it provides, and 
the role requirements.
2. Explain a time when you took personal initiative in a difficult situation.
I was asked a similar question in the interview as well. Keep an answer 
ready beforehand, as it can leave a very bad impression on the 
interviewer if you don’t even know about your accomplishments or 
anything difficult that you have done in your life so far.
3. For those who had applied for GMT, it was preferred that you complete the 
two coding questions, while it was not compulsory for the GBT role.
1) Given an array, find the sum of all numbers not divisible by 5 or 7.
A very simple question, that can be done by iterating over the 
array elements and adding to the sum only if num%5 != 0 and 
num%7 != 0. You had to take the array input by yourself though, we 
weren’t given any direct function where the array was passed. We 
also had to print the solutions to the console. I don’t remember 
exactly, but I think we had around 30 mins for this. I submitted it 
with 25 minutes left.
2) Given an array, find and print all distinct pairs that sum to a given 
target in ascending order.
Another standard question. I thought the brought force would 
definitely give TLE, so I went for the optimized approach using 
two-pointers. 
The code looked something like this:
We had to parse the input carefully. Each line was of the format:
2,3,4,12,19,22:36 -> Here the target and array are separated by 
the colon, so we first split using “:” and then we split using “,” 
and map it to an integer array. Since the list was already sorted, 
we start checking for sums of each pair and if the current sum is 
greater than the target, move the right pointer to the left and vice 
versa. Once this is done, print the output in the desired format. 
We had 45 minutes for this question, and I submitted it with 
around 30 minutes left. The third video question asked us to 
explain the approach we used to solve the previous questions and 
the alternate methods, their complexities, etc. I mentioned how 
the complexity drops to O(N) since we are making use of the fact 
that the array is sorted to limit the number of pairs we have to 
check.

3. Group discussion
All subsequent rounds were held offline. There were around 40 students, and we 
were divided into 4 groups with 10 students each. I was in group 4.
It was my first GD and I didn’t know what else to do apart from watching YouTube 
videos and reading articles regarding GD. It is also helpful to practice speaking as 
if you’re in a real GD - randomly take a topic and try to speak for an argument for 
at least one minute.
 Since the time taken was only 10-12 minutes per group, I only had one thing in 
mind - that it’s ok to speak only once or twice but I will make a unique point, or 
provide a counter perspective to someone else’s point. Speaking just for the heck 
of it is not useful at all and will probably get me negative judgment, so it’s best to 
formulate a point before speaking.
The topics are often general knowledge-based. The two topics I remember 
were “Cashless Economy”, “WFO vs WFH”, and “Role of AI in Finance”. Mine 
was simpler, “Social Media - a Boon or a Curse”.
There were six senior panelists and we were seated around benches facing them. 
They revealed the topic and told us that we may start the discussion now. 
Suddenly, 4-5 people, including me started to speak (intro ke points 🍭). 
Eventually, everyone went quiet and one girl gave the intro (I felt a bit dejected, 
but I’m not the end of the world. There’s plenty of time to make your mark). 2-3 
speakers later, I realized they were mostly negative, so when I got the chance I 
mentioned how social media has allowed many people like David Goggins to 
inspire others. I said something along the lines of social media is a double-edged 
sword, that it depends on the user whether it will be beneficial or not, and that 
social media is not to be blamed. A few minutes later I got irked when someone 
said that even young kids are so addicted to social media that they won’t even 
have food without it, start to cry, lose focus, it’s a drug etc etc 👹. So I tried to 
speak 4-5 times about that point (listening skill ke points 😋) and kept my hand 
raised. Finally, I said something like (with extensive hand gestures) “If one wants 
to waste time, one will find a way to waste time. A few years earlier, we would be 
discussing whether magazines are a nuisance or not. The instrument changes, 
but human behavior remains the same, hence that is to be blamed. Also, the kid 
being addicted is just an example of bad parenting and not social media being 
addictive”. Few of the panelists smiled as I spoke and I felt more confident (¬‿¬). 
That’s it, I only spoke twice.
Roughly 5 students were selected for the next round, and I was one of them 😎.
Prefer quality over quantity. There are examples where someone spoke 3-4 times 
but didn’t proceed, and where someone spoke only once but moved ahead. 
Remember, they aren’t here to see who can speak English the loudest.

3. Interview round
About 20 students had proceeded. Three interviews were conducted in parallel, 
by a pair of interviewers each (two for GPM, and one for GPT). I was feeling 
extremely nervous and underprepared. You would probably feel so too. It was my 
first, so I accepted it. Took a few deep breaths, rehearsed my intro one last time, 
and went in.
As I sat, they asked me how my day was and how I was feeling. I said that it was 
a wonderful morning, that I was feeling nervous but I like to tell myself that it’s 
exciting. They smiled and told me to introduce myself. After the intro, in which I 
mentioned at the end that I enjoy football, he asked me for my favorite club. I said 
Real Madrid. He said “Oh, a Real Madrid fan. Favorite player?” I said Cristiano 
Ronaldo and they laughed while saying “Of course”. 
Then, they took a look at my resume. The sir then said “I see you’ve been part of a 
few leadership positions at Pratibimb. What according to you makes a good 
leader?” This question threw me off a little because I was mostly expecting 
technical questions. I said, after a bit of fumbling, that a good leader makes the 
team “own” the project. The team has to understand that they’re not just 
organizing an event or completing their project, they are actually showcasing 
themselves. A good leader also makes sure to give personal attention to 
underperforming members, and also be polite yet firm regarding things. I 
expanded something along these lines.
He then asked me which language was my strongest among the ones I 
mentioned on my resume. I said Java. He told me to rate it, to which I gave an 8. 
It is better not to go above 8 I think, no matter how confident you feel.
He quickly withdrew a blank sheet of paper and started writing something. As 
he was writing, he asked if I was aware of error handling in Java to which I 
replied yes. Then he showed me the code he’d written: 
Try {
System.out.println(“In first block”);
Throw A;
} catch ( ExceptionTypeA e) {
System.out.println(e.getMessage());
Throw B;
} catch (ExceptionTypeB e) {
System.out.println(e.getMessage());
Throw C;
} finally {
System.out.println(“In finally block”);
Throw Z;
}
First, he asked me what would be the output of this, and what if ExceptionTypeB 
was a subclass of ExceptionTypeA 😳. I said that we wouldn’t get any output but 
rather a compiler error if we’re catching errors that are subclasses of some other 
error. I gave an example of first having a catch Exception block and second with a 
catch ArithmeticException block, how it would give an error since the Exception 
block would already catch exceptions of type ArithmeticException.
Then I looked at the code and said directly that Error Z would be thrown since 
the final block is always executed at the end. He then told me to go step by 
step and tell what happens with error C. I got very confused in between. A and B 
were caught so their statements were printed, but there was nothing for C, hence 
we should get a runtime error for C. But isn't the finally block the one that is 
always executed at the end? So what about Z? After thinking I said that I was not 
sure, but “In finally block” would be printed and Z would be thrown at the end. I do 
not know whether C will be thrown or not.
After this, he asked me to give some real-life use cases of try-catch blocks. I 
mentioned we may use the try block to make a request to our server, catch any 
network errors, and display them to the user, or do whatever we want. The finally 
block is generally used to free resources like database connections, so that 
whether or not the request was successful we make sure to free up the 
resources. He asked me, “What if I return some value in the try or exception 
block? Will it still be executed?” I replied yes. “What will be returned if all blocks 
are returning different values?” I said the value sent by the finally block will only 
be returned. “In what cases will the finally block not be executed?” I said we can 
use System.exit(), or if the JVM itself crashes only then will it not be executed.
Then he asked me if I was aware of multithreading. I gave a basic definition. He 
then asked me to implement it in Java. I was a bit taken aback, but I vaguely 
remembered an example I did while learning mergesort and wrote it down. It was 
something like this: 
class MergeSortThread extends Thread {
private int[] array;
public MergeSortThread(int[] array) {
        this.array = array;
}
    public void run() {
        mergeSort(array);
    }
Thread leftThread = new MergeSortThread(leftArray);
Thread rightThread = new MergeSortThread(rightArray);
leftThread.start();
rightThread.start();
leftThread.join();
rightThread.join();
I said that the Threads class in Java allows us to implement multithreading. He 
seemed satisfied with it, and just said that we usually put the join part in try catch 
for error handling.
He then asked me what type of algorithm is mergesort. I said it’s a sorting 
algorithm that uses the divide and conquer technique. He asked me if it was 
stable. I replied with yes since it doesn’t change the relative order of two entities 
if they have the same value. He asked me what algorithm is called if I use 
Arrays.sort(). I said that in Java, if the array is made of primitives then a double 
pivot quicksort is called. It’s unstable but doesn’t matter for primitives and is 
faster. For objects it uses “TimSort”, a combination of merge sort and insertion 
sort (I got really lucky with this question because I had done it just the night 
before). He seemed impressed and then asked me if I was aware of spring 
boot. I said that it’s used to develop web applications using Java, after which he 
told me to write a REST controller that exposes an endpoint /hello to return a 
greeting message. I said that I had never made something with spring boot. I only 
know its purpose. He said it’s fine. Looking back, I should’ve mentioned this the 
first time itself. But anyway, spring is quite uncommon amongst college students.
He then asked me if Java was a purely OOP language. I replied no, stating that for 
a pure OOP language, every data type must be user-defined and every method 
must be called through objects only. This is not the case because: 
1. The static keyword in Java allows us to access data or methods belonging 
to the class i.e. without the need of an object.
2. Primitives are not user-defined objects.
He then asked me, “But we use Integer as a class right? So doesn’t that make it 
an object?” I said that Integer, Double, Float, etc are wrapper classes that still use 
a primitive int, double, or float underneath. They are used to invoke certain 
functions like Integer.parseInt() etc that can’t be called via primitives like int. He 
then asked whether strings are primitive, to which I replied no. He asked if strings 
are mutable or not and to explain why. I said that strings are immutable in Java 
mainly due to storage optimization and safety. He then wrote this on the paper: 
String a = “abc”;
String b = new String(“abc”);
String c = “abc”;
println(a==b); print(a==c);
He asked me to explain the output. I said false for first and true for second, 
and drew this diagram: 
But with “abc”. I mentioned that we are saving memory by not creating new 
objects to store a string like “abc” but rather pointing to the same object in the 
pool. Using the “new” keyword normally allocates memory to the heap like any 
other object. I had watched this video previously.
After this, he asked me what I knew about equity derivatives. I was caught off 
guard and felt stupid for not reading about these things, considering I’m 
interviewing for a bank. I anxiously mumbled something about stocks and mutual 
funds. Then he asked me what is the process of buying a stock. I said that the 
exchange where the stocks are listed handles the transactions. To which he 
replied “No, what is the exact process? What happens when someone buys a 
stock?” I admitted I wasn’t aware of the underlying details. Next, she asked me 
what good coding practices one should follow. I gave examples of my project,
and said something along the lines of keeping your directory structure clean, 
giving descriptive variable/function names, keeping a simple and clean flow of 
data, etc.
He then asked me if I had any questions. I asked him the answer to the first 
question, and he explained that I was going in the correct direction - that the 
uncaught error would simply be ignored and only the final block error would be 
printed, after which the interview was over.
I wasn’t feeling too confident since I gave terrible responses to finance-related 
questions and many times they didn’t seem satisfied with my answers. But it was 
done, so I took a break and relaxed.
Once all the interviews were over, 9 students were shortlisted and luckily I was 
one of them.

4. HR round
There were six panelists for this interview. They told me to introduce myself and 
asked me a few basic questions regarding my family, what role my father has at 
his work, any hobbies, etc. Then, one of the senior panelists asked me why I 
wanted to work for a bank instead of some tech-specific company like TCS or 
Infosys. I said that banks require as much coding expertise as any other tech 
firm, if not more, as they have to handle data of millions of users, their 
transactions and need to have high levels of security as they deal with sensitive 
data. I mentioned some products like Bofa Mercury, Bofa electronic trading 
platform that I had read on their website, and said that these definitely require a 
lot of developers to maintain.
Now, I should’ve stopped here but I got carried away and said that firms like 
TCS are mainly involved in the outsourcing business, and banks probably 
outsource some projects to them for cheap labor (❁´◡`❁). They looked at each 
other and started laughing. Then he read my resume and said that you seem to 
have done a lot in Pratibimb, so give us your experience and what you learned 
from it. I said something about learning how to speak properly, managing 
extracurricular with academics (I said this only because I had a decent cgpa of 
8.9, otherwise you need to be careful with these statements😝), and working in a 
team. They asked me if I had plans for a master's, to which I said that I wanted to 
work and stay in India itself. Eventually, they asked if I had any questions for 
them. I asked, “I had read that people generally switch within a few years to get 
much larger salary hikes, so what made you stay at Bank of America for more 
than 35 years? If you had switched a few times, maybe you would’ve been at a 
higher compensation”. He started off by saying that there’s no right or wrong 
answer to whether you should stay or switch. He said that he did switch when he 
was younger, but he found more meaning in working and contributing to this 
place. He also mentioned that you get yearly raises at every company, and 
sometimes it’s okay to not want to leave a place where you enjoy working. With 
this, the interview ended. 
After an hour, the results were announced and I was one of the four selects 
(⌐■_■).

5. Conclusion
Here are certain things that might help you with your preparation: 
Technical
1) Pick a language and become a master at it, preferably the language you 
use DSA. 
2) Don’t focus too much on the quantity but the quality of your projects. Add 
new and unique features with time, so that it becomes really impressive at 
the end.
3) Always start DSA from the basics. I have wasted huge amounts of time 
trying to do tough problems, thinking that I am developing my 
“Problem-solving skills” which were clearly above my level. Certain 
problems cannot be solved by you without knowing the solution first. Your 
job is to comfortably understand basic algorithms like binary search, tree 
traversals, recursion, etc. Only then move on to tougher problems. 
4) It helped me a lot to perform a dry run on paper to understand the solution. 
I also tried to watch videos since the written explanations took a lot of time 
to understand.
5) You’ll have an easier time if you follow an order of doing topics. You may 
follow something like this:
Resources: Aditya Verma’s binary search and DP playlist, Striver’s array 
pisplaylist, and Love Babbar for trees and recursion. DSA 450 is a good collection 
of questions arranged in increasing difficulty. I liked Kunal Kushwaha’s videos for 
Java and oops.
Non-technical
1) Focus on making habits. Do the leetcode daily challenge, work and push 
changes to your project daily on github, and regularly google any new 
things you find. The only reason I knew about what function was used in 
Arrays.sort() was because I googled it out of curiosity. Same with many 
other concepts. You won’t get all the things perfectly placed in some 
playlist or article, so make this habit of learning anything new you find. You 
feel much less burdened if you immerse yourself in the learning process 
rather than always thinking about whether this will help you for internships 
or not.
2) Don’t be disheartened by failures. This was the first time ever that I could 
clear the online assessment and actually give an interview ;) No matter 
how well you do, there is always a factor of luck. So focus on what you can 
control - your preparation. Rest will be taken care of. Quoting James Clear 
here: “You do not rise to the level of your goals. You fall to the level of 
your systems.”
